paragraphs: The three hundred and seventy-two names were to be posted before Weiyang Palace the next day. Long after nightfall, fists were still striking desks in the western hall of the Secretariat.

The lampwicks had been trimmed three times. The water on the table had long since gone cold. The Vice Minister of Ceremonies flung the selection roll into the middle of the desk, exposing a muddy fingerprint on its first page. It was the mark made by Du Yuansheng, a waterworks official from Henei, when he attested to his record. When the Qin River rose the previous year, he had led men to cut open an old channel and saved seventeen riverside villages. Not one breach had appeared in the new embankments since. Yet he could write only ordinary official reports, and on his first visit to the palace he had even forgotten to unbuckle his sword.
“Such a man at the head of the list?” the vice minister demanded. “Is learning to count for nothing in this realm?”
Fu Hong pulled another document from the bottom of the bundle and laid it before him. “Look at his plans for the canal.”
The vice minister glanced at them. “I do not deny his achievements.”
“Then who deserves first place?”
“A man of literary standing.”
“From which family?”

The vice minister said no more. Several officials of the imperial clan looked equally displeased. Among the three hundred and seventy-two were former Han Chinese clerks, Xianbei cavalry officers, accountants from merchant households of Western Liang, Qiang men able to interpret two or three local tongues, and seven women bound for the medical and household offices. Only twenty-seven came from old distinguished Di families. That number had been an irritant among the clansmen for days.

“Our fathers and grandfathers helped the Heavenly King conquer Guanzhong,” said a white-bearded general. “Now their descendants must stand behind men of Former Yan. When Your Highness sends me home, what am I to tell my old comrades?”
Fu Hong opened a frontier army merit register. Its corners had curled, and black mud from a march still stained several pages.

“This list makes appointments; it does not strip anyone of inherited honors. Your second son applied to administer the camp registers. Of the thirty-seven households for which he reported relief payments last year, eleven names did not match the records and six households had never belonged to the camp. The examiners rejected him. If he disputes the decision, he may request a review.”
The general clenched his teeth. “A copying error by the clerks beneath him!”
“If so, the inquiry will clear his name. I have already ordered it reopened. Until the facts are established, I cannot put him on the list.”
Another official objected. “Du Yuansheng is a man without pedigree. Put him first today, and next year everyone will rush to learn canal-building. Who will still devote himself to the classics?”

An elderly clerk seated in the corner finally laughed aloud. “Waterworks require a knowledge of the current. Let them try it. When the rains come, which of them will stand beside a breach half the night?”

The argument was still raging when the night watch sounded beyond the palace. Fu Hong took up his brush and marked the last page for review. The sealed packet would go to the censors and then to the central secretariat for confirmation. The names would be posted as planned tomorrow. Having said this, he rose and left. The clansmen were still calling after him. As an attendant shut the doors, he saw the lamplight of the western hall falling across the bent figures of the old men.
In the rear palace, Fu Rong was moving a wine cup away from Fu Jian’s hand.
“The palace physicians told you to drink less.”
“It is medicinal wine.”
“Where is the medicine?”
“In the wine.”

Fu Rong poured it into a bronze basin. Fu Jian glanced at him without trying to stop him, then continued leafing through the general register of replacement household entries for Hebei. Of late he had found it difficult to sit for long. His right wrist trembled when he wrote, and a long felt cushion now lay beside his desk so he could lean against it when tired.
“Will you go to see the list tomorrow?” Fu Rong asked.
“I will.”
“Some clansmen have already threatened to kneel in protest before the hall.”
“Let them kneel. It is cold. See that they have hot soup.”
Fu Rong sat beside the couch. Neither brother spoke for a while. The watch drum came through three palace gates, faint as an echo from another year.
“Do you really trust that list?” Fu Jian asked suddenly.
“I trust that Du Yuansheng has built canals.”
“And if he takes bribes from the river contractors next year?”
“Investigate him.”
“And if the investigator takes bribes?”
“Investigate again.” Fu Rong smiled. “These days, when Your Majesty questions a man, you would have every lawsuit of the next thirty years tried before morning.”

Fu Jian laughed too, then coughed several times. Fu Rong drew the heavy cloak closer about his shoulders. His fingers brushed a protruding collarbone, and his heart sank, though his voice remained teasing. “If you faint in public tomorrow, I will not take the ritual officers' scolding for you.”
“I will make no long proclamation. I only wish to see the people.”
“Then we may be spared that.”

Before dawn the next day, the square before Weiyang Palace was crowded with people awaiting the names. Some had ridden from Longyou, their felt boots white with salt; others had lodged in straw sheds outside the city and come in darkness to claim a place. A tall, thin man from Henei kept trying to straighten his cap at the palace gate, making it more crooked every time. Those around him recognized Du Yuansheng and showed him how to bring the ties beneath his ears.
“You can reckon the head of a flood, but you cannot put on an official’s cap?” someone teased.
Du Yuansheng pulled the knot tight, sweating. “A broken canal can be repaired. If my cap falls, all Chang’an will see it.”

In one corner of the crowd Helai A-Luo stood with the students of the commandery school. He had an inkstone tucked into his sleeve; he planned to buy paper for his teacher on the way back. Fu Sheng, with whom he had once fought, was there too, muttering all the way about whose forebears had commanded troops in which province. A-Luo did not trouble to argue. He looked only toward the list. On it were two clerks from his commandery and a man who had once interpreted for Qiang households in New Citizens' Ward at Weichang.

Bronze horns sounded at the palace gate. Fu Jian arrived in his carriage, with Fu Hong and Fu Rong standing on either side. Murong Chui wore a dark blue-green official robe with only his newly issued seal of office at his waist. Fu Pi stood on the other side; an old scar at his temple showed faintly in the winter light. The masters of ceremony had first assigned the two men separate places, but someone had changed the arrangement, so they stood not far apart. Fu Pi glanced at Murong Chui, who merely inclined his head.
Three wooden cases were opened and verified in succession. The clerks hung the sheets, and a long voice began calling the names before Weiyang Palace.
“Du Yuansheng of Henei, appointed Deputy Director of the River and Canal Office.”

Du Yuansheng could not decide whether to walk forward or kneel first. Two men beside him gave him a shove. As he stepped out, his cap nearly fell, and laughter swept across the square. Fu Jian laughed as well. Holding the carriage rail, he told him, “If another canal bursts, I will not accept that official cap of yours in payment for the damage.”
Du Yuansheng knocked his head against the ground. “I beg Your Majesty to take my plans, not my cap.”
When the laughter subsided, the reading continued. At the twenty-first name a rustle suddenly moved through the crowd.
“Liang Agui of Anding, appointed Camp Register Officer of Beidi.”

Liang Agui stepped forward, limping slightly from an arrow wound to his right leg at White Horse Slope. Once he had known only how to carve grain tallies and wounded soldiers' names into wooden boards; now he could read registers and write official documents himself. Before accepting his appointment scroll, he looked up and asked, “My younger brother Liang Abao is still serving his sentence. As a camp register officer, may I see the judgment against him?”
The ritual officer’s face changed. Fu Jian looked at the man. “You may.”
“And if the judgment was unjust?”
“You may appeal.”
“And if it was just?”
“Then he must serve his full term.”
Liang Agui accepted the answer. He was about to return to his place when a woman screamed from the western corridor.

The crossbow snapped, sharp as a stalk of bamboo breaking under strain. Fu Pi, standing nearer, saw a dark blue-black flicker behind Liang Agui’s shoulder. Before he could shout he had hurled himself against the man and knocked him down. The bolt cut through the spot where they had stood, grazed Fu Pi’s shoulder, and struck the list board hard, pinning down a sheet through the words “relief for families.”

The crowd surged outward. Palace soldiers drew their swords and patrol guards sealed the western corridor. A boy carrying a book case was knocked down. A-Luo reached to pull him up and realized it was Fu Sheng. Both fell into the same cloud of dust. White-faced, Fu Sheng asked, “Will they arrest our Fu family?”
“Get up first,” said A-Luo. Only when the other was standing did he answer. “They should arrest whoever fired the bolt.”

Before the board, Fu Hong was already stopping a junior clerk from tearing away the paper. “Do not touch it! Mark where the bolt went in.” A censor crouched on the ground making a diagram. Fu Rong secured the royal carriage; Murong Chui personally led the search of the corridor. Fu Pi tore a sleeve from his own robe and pressed it to the wound, yet still snapped at Liang Agui, kneeling on the ground: “If you’re unhurt, stand up. Who are you kneeling for?”
“Your Highness saved my life.”
“They read your name a moment ago. My ears still work.”
“I am Qiang, Your Highness.”
“I know.” Fu Pi looked at him. “Should Qiang blood be spilled on my father’s list, then?”

By the time the physician arrived, blood from Fu Pi’s shoulder had stained half his collar. The cut was shallow but long, and hurt whenever he moved. Liang Agui tried once more to thank him, but Fu Pi pushed him toward a guard. “Finish checking the Beidi camp registers. You may thank me then.”

The would-be assassin never escaped the western corridor. He was a Di military-household man in his twenties named Fu Gui, formerly an armory clerk, who had failed a selection examination in his commandery. On him the guards found a crumpled sheet calling Qiang people slaves and claiming that the rewards for founding the dynasty belonged solely to Di households. The small crossbow had a cleverly fashioned mechanism and a military craftsman’s mark; its provenance had yet to be proved. Fu Gui clenched his teeth and refused to say who had obtained the weapon for him.
Someone before the hall called for the announcement to be halted. Fu Jian was about to speak when Fu Pi raised his bandaged hand. “Read on.”
“Your Highness has lost blood...”
“Read on.” He looked at the elderly clansmen crowding around him. “If we withdraw the list for this scratch on my skin, tomorrow the next man who dislikes it will only have to borrow a crossbow.”

The master of ceremony hesitated. Fu Rong tightened Fu Pi’s bandage, cursed his show of bravado under his breath, then turned and ordered the names read aloud. All three hundred and seventy-two had been announced by afternoon. Last came a veterinarian from the Dai frontier skilled in treating epidemics among horses. The man had not arrived, so village elders accepted the appointment for him. When the final name was read, no one cheered. All eyes remained on the bolt still lodged in the board.

Fu Jian ordered the appointees and ministers into the hall. The pierced noticeboard was left where it stood, roped off and placed under the censors' personal guard. The afternoon’s arguments inside Weiyang Palace were fiercer than those of the night before. Some wanted every imperial-clan estate searched; others proposed striking every Qiang name from the list to calm public anger. Still others seized the confusion to demand control of garrisons in Beidi.

Fu Jian listened for half the day, coughing until he had to lean back. Du Yuansheng sat by the doorway, the cords of his official cap drawing red lines across his neck. Finally he could bear no more and muttered, “If the court goes on debating like this, the canals will not be ready for the spring flood.”
Murong Chui heard him and turned. “Deputy Director Du, how would you deal with the assassin?”
Du Yuansheng scrambled to his feet. “I do not know how to deal with assassins, my lord. I know how to repair sluices.”
“Then speak of sluices.”
“If someone breaks a gate, you must catch the man who broke it. But if the timber has rotted, you must replace that too. Otherwise, catch ten men and the water will still leak.”
“Which timber in this list has rotted?”

Du Yuansheng thought for some time. “Those who failed cannot see how the examiners measured them. They will always suspect that someone paid for a place. The list gives results alone. It is like watching another family’s water flow through a canal without knowing when your own turn comes. Perhaps the evidence behind the assessments should be posted where people can inspect it and check the accounts for themselves.”

His words came haltingly, and several ministers dismissed them. But Fu Hong asked him to stay. The Secretariat at once drafted a proposal to disclose verifiable achievements and the names of sponsors, with a fixed period for appeal. Frontier secrets and witnesses' families would still receive the protection prescribed by law; everything could not simply be posted in public. Fu Jian ordered the provinces to discuss the proposal before any decision. No statute was to be hurried into force on account of that day’s arrow.
Then an old Di general rose. His hair was entirely white, his armor still bore a sword scar from the days of Shi Hu, and his voice shook.

“Your Majesty, you once promised that those who shed blood beside you would share in prosperity. We are old now. Some of our fields have been measured away, and our grandsons are laughed at beneath the list. Did the brothers who died in Guanzhong all die for nothing?”

Fu Jian ordered a seat brought for him. The old soldier refused it, standing with a hand braced on his knee. Fu Jian let him speak the names of the dead without interruption. Only after he had caught his breath did the king reply, “I did make that promise. If anyone has withheld the lawful lands or pay of the old troops, or the relief due to the war dead, bring the matter before the censors. But even for one man’s service, I cannot promise that his grandson need do nothing and still take the future that belongs to others.”

The old general stared at him. His lips moved twice, yet he said nothing. Candlelight fell on his graying temples. Fu Rong noticed that the hand resting on the desk never stopped trembling. Without offering thanks, the old man turned back toward his place and nearly fell as he grasped the table. Fu Rong hurried over and helped him sit.
Only then did Murong Chui rise. By the time he spoke, the hall had grown much quieter.

“Old merit cannot entitle a family to command soldiers forever. Nor can the former kingdom of Yan claim Ye as private property for all time merely because it once ruled there. What, then, of the Fu family’s throne in the years to come?”
A clansman slapped the table. Fu Jian raised a hand to silence him.
“Are you asking when I shall abolish hereditary rule?”
“I am asking whom Your Majesty means to leave that problem to.”

“To those still alive,” Fu Jian said. “If I announced today that the throne of Heavenly King no longer belonged to the Fu family, every province of the North would raise its former ruler tomorrow. Who would defend the Huai? Who would protect these newly registered military households?”
“And ten years from now?”

Fu Jian looked at him without offering a pleasing, easy deadline. He said only that the imperial clan might not maintain great private armies; those who broke the law would be tried under the law; and the appointment or removal of an heir must not be settled by a secret edict from a sickbed. Fu Hong stood beside him, quietly taking notes. Fu Pi held his injured shoulder and said nothing.
“As for what comes after,” Fu Jian said softly, “I dare not write the future for those who follow us.”

Murong Chui bowed, showing neither pleasure nor displeasure. When the council broke up, Fu Pi came across Liang Agui in the corridor. The man stopped as soon as he saw him and saluted with clasped hands. Fu Pi asked why he had not gone to collect his official seal.
“I wanted to see where the bolt came from.”
“The case is not closed.”
“That is why I must remember.”

Fu Pi beckoned him nearer and laid his uninjured hand on the scroll of appointment. “If, after taking office, you fail to pay one household its relief, the bolt I took for you today will have been taken for nothing.”
Liang Agui tucked the appointment into his robe. His throat moved, but he did not offer another speech of thanks. He gave Fu Pi a soldier’s salute, not the obeisance owed to a prince.

By night Fu Jian was too weary to walk unaided. Fu Hong accompanied him to the rear palace. The old dispute over military lands in the North remained unresolved, and several villages without proper registration in Hebei were still fighting over water. Yet another secret report had arrived from Jiangnan: the influence of the old disciples of the Xie family was waning, the Beifu Army lacked pay, and the garrisons of Jingzhou were each maneuvering for more soldiers. Xie An and Xie Xuan were both gone, yet their juniors in Jiankang still invoked their names in disputes over affairs of state.
After hearing the report, Fu Jian reached for a map of the Huai River. Fu Hong spread it out for him. “Father, do you still wish to cross the Yangtze?”

Fu Jian ran a finger over the fine line of water on the map. Once he had thought there was only a river between him and the unfinished triumph of his life. Now, beside the map, lay a report of vacant offices in Beidi, military pay overdue at Luoyang, and a selection list pierced by a crossbow bolt. Each held his hand where it was, for the moment.
“We will not cross today,” Fu Jian said.

Fu Hong did not press him to say when. Beyond the window a wind swept over the palace wall and billowed the newly posted sheets. The bolt was still in the censors' keeping; a small hole remained in the wooden board. Outside the hall, Du Yuansheng was busy disputing next spring’s timber accounts with an envoy from Henei. Liang Agui, his new seal against his chest, first went to army headquarters to request the old judgment against his younger brother Liang Abao. When a clerk asked whether he wished his brother’s case reviewed ahead of the others, he said they must proceed in the order the petitions had been received. An hour later he was still standing under the eaves with an old woman from another family, the old arrow wound in his foot aching again in the cold. Far away in Ye, the schoolroom lamps in New Citizens' Ward remained lit. A-Luo copied the county’s new household-transfer register until midnight. Hearing a neighbor’s child cry, he put down his brush and went to ask whether another quarrel had broken out over the water turns.

The lamps of Weiyang Palace went dark one by one. Three still burned in the Secretariat’s western hall. There, a clerk had spread out the registers for tomorrow’s review and laid paperweights on their curling corners. The night watch clerk called out that dawn was near. The man at the desk answered without lifting his brush.
